title: Boot Into Your Code: Service Units From a Spec, the Order They Start In, and a Crash Loop With and Without a Back-Off

questions.question: What does Requires=drivers say about the order of start?
options: That drivers is started first
Nothing: it says the service cannot run without drivers, and the order needs After as well
That the two are started at the same moment
That drivers restarts the service if it fails
questions.explanation: Requires is about dependence and After is about order. With only Requires the two start together, and the planner finds nothing on half the boots.

questions.question: A service crashes 0.2 s after every start and is restarted after 0.1 s with no limit. How many starts in 60 s?
options: About 200 (201 in the run), and the log and a core are busy with it
5, the default limit
6, one every ten seconds
1: a crashed service is not restarted
questions.explanation: A crash at 0.2 s and a restart after 0.1 s is about three starts a second. The broken program fills the log and keeps a core busy for as long as it is left.

questions.question: The same crash with a start limit of 5 in 10 s and a restart of 0.1 s. What happens?
options: It restarts for ever, a little slower
It backs off to once every 30 s
It gives up at 1.5 s after five starts, and the robot is without that program until somebody notices
It is restarted 201 times
questions.explanation: Five starts in a second and a half reach the limit, and the service is left failed. The robot goes on without that program.

questions.question: What does a back-off of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 30 s do for the same crash?
options: Two hundred starts, spread over the minute
It gives up after five starts
Nothing: the waits are ignored once the limit is set
Six starts in a minute, and the start limit is never reached because the starts are far apart
questions.explanation: Each wait is longer than the last, so a persistent fault costs a handful of starts and the service is still being tried.

questions.question: Why should a back-off reset after a long stable run?
options: To keep the waits from overflowing
A service healthy for a day that crashes once should restart at once, not wait 30 s for crashes from its first minute
Because the start limit is counted per day
So that the log shows the first crash
questions.explanation: The back-off answers a crash loop. A long healthy run means the loop is over, and the next crash is a new event.

questions.question: A safety-relevant service is given up on by the init system. What should happen?
options: Nothing: the init system has dealt with it
A reboot, which starts everything again
A restart of that service only
A stop: a robot that moves and cannot see is the worst combination, and the supervisor of lesson 19-10 has to see it
questions.explanation: A service that was given up on is no longer doing its job. If that job was seeing obstacles, the supervisor has to know and stop the robot.
